big: Meena asked for her money back a week ago and nothing has arrived. She is worried and angry. There is a clear route for this, and each step has a reason. Skipping to the top is the usual mistake.

lines: My redemption has not arrived in a week. Who do I complain to?
There is an order to it. Let us climb it one step at a time.

alt: Three boxes: fund house, SCORES, ODR, joined by arrows
caps: Step 1: write to the fund house's investor service team. Note the reference number.
Step 2: if the reply is late or not satisfactory, complain on SEBI's platform, SCORES.
Step 3: if it is still unresolved, SEBI's online dispute resolution, ODR, is the next step.
Most issues end at step 1. Keep every reference number as you climb.

title: Keep a paper trail
stops: A phone call needs no written trace
Only the fund house should keep records
alt: A shield with what records help a complaint and what does not
caps: Good records protect everyone: you, the client and the adviser.
Keep application copies, statements, reference numbers and notes of what was discussed.
A phone call with no written trace is hard to prove, and unclaimed money needs current KYC and bank details.

q: Meena's redemption has not arrived after a week. She wants to go straight to SEBI. What does the adviser suggest first?
opts: Go straight to court, since even a delay of a week is already wrong
Write to the fund house's investor service team and note the reference
Wait another month or so, as such delays usually sort themselves out
Complain only to the distributor, as the fund house cannot help her
why: A court case is slow and costly, and it skips the simple steps that often solve the matter quickly.
Most issues end at the fund house, and its reference number is needed if she has to escalate later.
Waiting without writing leaves no record. She should raise it now, in writing, and note the reference.
The fund house holds her redemption record, so it is the right first stop. A distributor cannot fix a payout.

q: Meena wrote to the fund house and was promised a reply within a week. Two weeks later there is nothing. What next?
opts: Ask another fund house's investor service team to step in
Write the same letter again and wait for another month or so
Close the folio and write off the amount as not worth it
File on SEBI's SCORES platform, where complaints are tracked
why: Another fund house holds none of her records and has no power over her fund. SCORES is the escalation route.
Repeating the letter gives the fund house more time but no escalation. It adds no new record or pressure.
Closing the folio does not cure the problem. The money is still owed to her, and she should claim it.
After a late or unsatisfactory reply, SCORES is the next step, and complaints there are tracked against timelines.

q: A dividend cheque came back because Dadi's old bank account was closed. Where does the money sit now?
opts: It is lost for good, since a returned cheque cannot be reissued
With SEBI, which pays it out on its own after a year
With the fund house as unclaimed money, claimable with proof
With her old bank, which must be asked to reopen the account
why: The money is not lost. It stays claimable with proof of identity and current bank details.
SEBI does not hold investors' money, and it pays nothing out on its own. The fund house keeps it for her.
Unclaimed amounts sit with the fund house and can be claimed with proof. Her KYC and bank details must be current.
A closed account cannot receive it, and the bank never held it. She should update her details with the fund house.

q: A year later a client says: you told me this fund was guaranteed. What protects both client and adviser?
opts: A verbal promise from the client never to raise it again
Nothing can help, since it is one person's word against another's
Only the fund house's own records, since advisers need none
Copies of the application and statements, plus notes of the meeting
why: A spoken promise adds no proof and cannot stop a complaint. A written record is what helps.
Without records it is one word against another. Writing things down is exactly what removes that problem.
The fund house cannot know what was said in the meeting. Advisers need their own notes and copies of papers.
Notes of the discussion show what was said, and application copies show what was signed. Both protect everyone.

pts: Fund house first, and keep the reference number.
Then SEBI's SCORES platform, and ODR if that does not work.
Keep every record: applications, statements, reference numbers and notes.
